Issued at 334 AM CDT Sun Sep 6 2026

Summary: 

The large scale pattern evolution across CONUS remains a generally 
broken record, with continued high confidence in its evolution over 
the next few days. Just peek the LREF 500mb spreads for confirmation 
in that regard. The existing Omega Block pattern will finally begin 
to break down later today and into the work week, but substantial 
and widespread relief from the existing heat is unlikely before mid-
week. In fact, a brief resurgence of heat is expected Tuesday. In 
the more immediate, chances for showers and storms remain today, 
including the potential for a few strong to severe and even some 
localized heavy rainfall. 

Heat and Eventual Relief:

With the mid-level ridge entrenched over central CONUS, the immediate 
area unsurprisingly remains very quiet at the moment. The advertised 
cool front has made its way into and across much of the CWA, as seen 
by the light E to NE winds. Unfortunately for western areas of the 
CWA though is that notable relief (cooler temps and lower dew 
points) remain displaced further east. In fact, there is actually a 
ribbon of enhanced dew points across the state currently with the 
drier airmass yet back into Illinois. This will help, to some 
degree, set the table for shower/storm chances later today, but more 
on that in a minute. 

The large surface high responsible for the easterly winds will 
continue to drop into the Great Lakes Region, but given its position, 
remains unexpected to push much additional relief across the state 
as it should effectively stall in/around the Kansas-Missouri border. 
This will result in temperatures today ranging from the upper 80s to 
low 90s in NE Missouri to more of the same mid-upper 90s to around 
100 for western and central Missouri and heat index values 
approaching 105 to 110. Monday temps may be a couple degrees cooler, 
but still seasonally well above normal, as the easterly winds 
struggle to provide much tangible temperatures or dew point relief 
beyond eastern Missouri. As the Omega Block breaks down, the mid-
level ridge shifts back eastward and begins to flatten, heat does 
briefly surge back on Tuesday when 850mb temps peak. That may yield 
yet one more day in the mid-upper 90s to 100 for much of the CWA. 
Given the above, Extreme Heat Warnings remain for areas around/south 
of Highway 36 through today/Sunday and in/around the Kansas City 
metro through Tuesday. An additional short duration headline for 
areas outside of the Kansas City metro counties may be considered 
for Tuesday. 

By Wednesday, the western CONUS cutoff low will have tracked into 
the Canadian Plains, flattening the mid-level ridge. Its attendant 
surface low will have pushed a cold front across the Northern to 
Central Plains, likely to approach northern Missouri by Wednesday 
morning. There remains a little uncertainty in timing and how 
quickly it pushes southward across the state, which may result in a 
bifurcated CWA when it comes to highs Wednesday. Regardless, by 
Thursday more seasonable temperatures are anticipated for most, 
while southern areas toward central Missouri may remain a few 
degrees above normal. Southerly winds return to end the week into 
the weekend, likely to bounce temperatures back warmer a few degrees 
but not to the extent we have experienced of late. 

Shower and Storm Chances: 

For today, an interesting evolution in CAM guidance overnight and 
early this morning. HRRR/RAP guidance has tended to scale back the 
area coverage and potential for air-mass convection this afternoon. 
Now largely relegating those opportunities just W and SW of the CWA. 
This appears to be at least partially in response to anticipated 
cloud cover overspreading the area from existing Nebraska 
convection, which would temper peak mixing. Recent HRRR runs depict 
more cloud cover over eastern Kansas than is reality, areas 
in/around KC Metro may yet see some air mass thunderstorms. Any such 
storms would be within an environment characterized by weak wind 
profiles and sizable inverted-V (large DCAPE) profiles. This should 
yield a primary threat for strong to damaging winds from 
evaporatively enhanced downdrafts and brief non-severe hail during 
peak heating. Additionally, the aforementioned Nebraska convection 
is expected to continue into Iowa and given the position of the mid-
level ridge axis and CAPE gradient, may drift down into northern 
Missouri. Recent CAM trends suggest much of the activity remains in 
Iowa given the more E to ESE deep layer sheer/steering profiles, but 
cannot rule it out especially should a cold pool/outflow move into 
the area. Damaging winds would likely remain the primary threat, but 
depicted better deep (speed) shear could allow for a severe hail 
threat as well. There is an SPC Day 1 Marginal Risk for severe 
storms given all of the above. There is also a WPC Excessive
